clues.title: Warning sign: Warning Signs

clues.title: Pole: Pole Warning Signs
text: The yellow warning stickers on utility poles can be a good way to distinguish between the UK and Ireland.
The most important difference is that UK stickers feature a guy getting zapped by a lightning bolt.
The Irish stickers usually have a lightning bolt, but lack the guy getting zapped.
They also often have an extra second rectangular sticker with a black outline, below the lightning bolt.

clues.title: Bollard: Scotland Bollard
text: In Scotland, you can often find these red and white bollards. They are round, bulky, and have a red-and-grey reflector that wraps all the way around.
They are sometimes found in other parts of the UK.
**NOTE:** The bollard looks similar to the French one. However, there are some small differences. For example, the Scottish bollard is round on the top, while the French one is more spiked.

clues.title: Architecture: Identical Look
text: Suburbs in UK towns tend to have a recognizable look.
They typically feature near-identical houses, often semi-detached, usually with well-manicured lawns.
The road layout can be maze-like, with lots of cul-de-sacs and curvy roads.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Chimney Pots
text: Many British buildings have distinct-looking chimneys with multiple so-called chimney pots.
These pots are usually round and brick-coloured.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Timber Framing
text: Some buildings, both old and new, feature black-and-white timber framing.
This is less common in Ireland.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Red Bricks
text: Red brick buildings are common in many parts of the UK.
Red brick architecture is also common in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Denmark, as well as parts of northern France.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Terraced Houses
text: Terraced houses (row houses) are very common in the UK.
This housing type shares walls on both sides with neighbouring homes.
You will also see a lot of semi-detached houses, which share just one side wall with another house.
61% of the population lives in terraced or semi-detached houses, significantly more than most other European countries

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Scotland - Sandstone & Granite
text: It is common to see houses made of large blocks of sandstone or granite in Scotland.
Granite buildings are common in Aberdeen, red sandstone is common in Glasgow and Dumfries, and yellow sandstone is common in Edinburgh.

clues.title: A9 Roads
text: The main A-roads in the UK are grouped by their first digit after the A, for example A380 will be located in the southwest of the country.
Beware that A-roads starting with any digit from 1 to 8 can also be found in Northern Ireland.
Tip: Imagine the UK as a clock, the digits go clockwise, starting at 1 and ending at 9.

text: The Scottish Highlands can be distinguished by the semi-barren, very mountainous landscape.
NOTE: A lot of Generation 4 coverage in the Highlands is from (early) spring, meaning that the vegetation often looks brown and yellow.
In addition, some of the most mountainous parts of Wales and Northern England can look similar.

clues.title: Sign: Scotland - Passing place sign
text: These ‘Passing Place’ signs are 95% found in Scotland. Wales has Welsh written under it and the England version is the same.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Wales - ARAF road marking
text: In Wales, markings on the road are in both English and Welsh. One of the best examples of this is ‘Araf’, which means ‘Slow’. This marking is only found in Wales.
NOTE: Araf is not the only Welsh language marking you can find, it is just the most common. Whenever you see an obviously non-English marking next to an English one, consider guessing in Wales.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Wales - Welsh language
text: Welsh is a Celtic language that is spoken throughout Wales. Road signs in Wales are usually bilingual English and Welsh. Towns often have Welsh names too. Welsh uses the letters D, W, and Y much more commonly than English. The double LL is also very distinct.
NOTE: Scottish Gaelic and Irish are both also Celtic languages. They can look somewhat similar to Welsh.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Northern Ireland - Black sticker with yellow text
text: These black stickers with yellow text sometimes appear on lampposts in Northern Ireland.
NOTE: Wiltshire have the same stickers on lamposts, so be aware of that.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Vegetation: Cornish palms
text: Cornish palms (Cordyline australis) in the UK are most commonly found in the far southwest along the coast and in Jersey. Although, they can rarely be found all along the west coast up to Scotland.

clues.title: Street sign: Aberdeenshire + Aberdeen street sign

clues.title: Cylindrical hay bales
text: Cylindrical hay bales laying around on these hilly agricultural fields can mostly be found in the region north of Aberdeen. They can very rarely be seen elsewhere in Scotland.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Snowdonia
text: Some roads, mostly in the south and north Snowdonia, have these distinct dark grey stone walls with vertical stones on top of it along the road. The landscape itself is very forested and mountainous, but less forested in the north east.
NOTE: These stone walls can be found elsewhere too, most commonly in North Wales.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Scotland - Scottish Gaelic
text: Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language that is closely related to Irish. They have a very similar look and use accent marks commonly. Common and recognizable letter clusters include bh, dh, fh, mh, ai, ea, eo, and ui.
Scottish Gaelic on road signs is found most commonly in the Scottish Highlands, and is almost always found north of Glasgow.
NOTE: Scottish Gaelic on road signs will often be in green or yellow text. This will not happen with Welsh or Irish on road signs.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Coverage: Boat trekker
text: Boat trekkers are limited to three locations: the River Thames, which runs through London, Keyhaven Lake, and Loch Ness lake. Each have different boats and very different landscapes.

Derby always has 7 letters/numbers and no space between the text and diamond.

clues.title: Language: Welsh
text: Welsh is a Celtic language spoken throughout Wales. Road signs in Wales are usually bilingual English and Welsh. Towns often have Welsh names too.
Welsh uses the letters **D, W**, and **Y** much more commonly than English. The double **LL** is also very distinct.
In Wales, markings on the road are in both English and Welsh. One of the best examples of this is **Araf**, which means Slow. This marking is only found in Wales.
NOTE: Scottish Gaelic and Irish are both also Celtic languages. They can look somewhat similar to Welsh.

clues.title: Language: Scottish Gaelic
text: Scottish Gaelic is a Celtic language closely related to Irish. They have a very similar look and use accent marks commonly. Common and recognizable letter clusters include **bh, dh, fh, mh, ai, ea, eo**, and **ui**.
Scottish Gaelic on road signs is found most commonly in the Scottish Highlands, and is almost always found north of Glasgow.
NOTE: Scottish Gaelic on road signs will often be in green or yellow text. This will not happen with Welsh or Irish on road signs.

clues.title: Language: English
text: English is the main language of the United Kingdom (I bet you knew that already). Keep in mind that English is also spoken in Ireland, aswell as Malta and Gibraltar within Europe. It is not uncommon to find English in other countries aswell, where is acts as an international language.
